newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis ends fourth week with gunfire.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis ends fourth week with gunfire.

text.p: Peru's hostage crisis ended its fourth week deadlocked as Marxist rebels holding 74 captives underlined their defiant stand by firing three bursts of gunfire into the air.

With direct talks between the government and Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels bogged down in uncompromising positions, the gunmen holed up inside the Japanese ambassador's home gave another warning on Monday of their armed presence.
Witnesses and policemen said they believed the rebels used assault rifles to fire into the air from within the residence after spotting what appeared to be a police helicopter hovering overhead.
"The helicopter came too close, so they opened fire," one policeman at the site told Reuters.
The shots sent birds scattering in panic across the front of the residence and police crouched in alert positions, weapons at the ready.
Red Cross officials later confirmed that the shots had caused no injuries.

The gunfire did nothing to sway President Alberto Fujimori from his tough line with the roughly 15 rebels who stormed a lavish reception at the residence on Dec. 17 and took hundreds of guests hostage.

"Our position and attitude is not to give in to their threat but to leave open the possibility of a peaceful end. The international community has supported this position," state news agency Andina quoted Fujimori as saying during a dinner with visiting Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram.
The MRTA has released most of the more than 500 hostages they seized in what they called "goodwill gestures."

It hopes to use those who remain -- including dozens of Peruvian government and security force officials, the younger brother of Fujimori and Japanese businessmen and diplomats -- as bargaining chips to secure their main demand for the release of more than 400 jailed comrades.

Fujimori has repeatedly ruled out considering this demand, dismissing it as "terrorist blackmail." But he has floated the possibility of transporting the rebels to another country if they lay down their arms and release all of their captives.

"My government's immovable position from the start is that we will not release prisoners. Why would we free terrorists? We're negotiating safe passage, and there are various ways to do that," Fujimori told the weekly U.S. news magazine Time in an interview published on Monday.
With both sides refusing to back down, negotiations continued through the exchange of notes and messages written on crude signs.

A planned meeting between government negotiator Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa inside the residence was called off on Sunday after the rebel insisted talks be centred on his demand that MRTA prisoners be released.
Palermo sent a written reply to Cerpa proposing the creation of a "guarantor committee" to oversee talks to end the crisis.

Using its now familiar mode of communication, the rebels placed a placard in an upper window of the residence asking Palermo to allow a local television network to enter the building to enable the MRTA to "make a public reply to the proposal."
There was no immediate response from the government.

Monday's gunfire at the residence was the latest in a series of diplays of force by the rebels. They are armed with assault rifles and grenades and have booby trapped and mined the diplomatic compound against a surprise attack.
In his interview with Time, Fujimori said that "no one can tell how long this (crisis) could go on," adding that he could not rule out the use of force on either side.
